name: Topaz (Ruby on RPython)
workload: 13 Benchmarks-Game-style single-threaded programs (binarytrees, brainfuck, brainfuck2, fannkuchredux, fasta, knucleotide, mandelbrot, matmul, nbody, pidigits, regexdna, revcomp, spectralnorm), best of up to 5 runs, in Docker; Topaz is the RPython tracing-JIT build of the kostya/topaz fork.
claimed_speedup: Faster than CRuby 2.7.7 on 12 of 13 programs (derived from page data): binarytrees 1.97 s vs 6.75 s, mandelbrot 1.47 s vs 16.74 s, nbody 5.42 s vs 43.56 s, spectralnorm 1.44 s vs 17.18 s, matmul 1.83 s vs 18.39 s, brainfuck 17.41 s vs 115.31 s; slower only on revcomp (7.3 s vs 4.2 s).
compiler_and_flags: Topaz translated with PyPy 2.7 v7.3.6 `rpython -Ojit targettopaz.py` (docker/topaz in the shootout repo); CRuby 2.7.7 built with `./configure --disable-install-doc --disable-install-rdoc --disable-install-capi` on ubuntu:22.10 with gcc 12.2.0 (docker/ruby2).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10 (README states tested on x86_64 and Apple M1; round 1 results dated 2023-02-28)
tradeoffs: docs/current-status.rst: implements Ruby 1.9.3 only, not stable, 'extremely incomplete': most of the standard library missing, no threading, no call/cc, no private method visibility. Building needs a PyPy source checkout and the RPython toolchain; README says the JIT translation takes 5-10 minutes.
caveats: The shootout ran the kostya/topaz fork (8 stars; its page says it updates to a newer PyPy and swaps in a faster default hash implementation), not topazproject/topaz itself; the fork page says the original repo has not been developed since 2016 and its last commit page shows 2022-06-18. Baseline is CRuby 2.7.7 (the same shootout lists Ruby 3.2.1 rows separately); Ruby 1.9.3 semantics mean the programs exercise only a small slice of the language. Single benchmark author, one machine, one round. Found by harvesting a row from a shootout, not from a Topaz-authored claim.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'tracing JIT Python OR Ruby OR PHP faster than PyPy benchmark blog open source new JIT compiler 2026' surfaced kostya/jit-benchmarks; the Topaz rows were read from its README tables and docker/topaz, docker/ruby2, tools/languages.rb.

name: JRuby
workload: Same 13 single-threaded Benchmarks-Game-style programs as the Topaz entry (JRuby 9.4.1.0 on OpenJDK 19.0.1, default flags and `-Xcompile.invokedynamic=true`), best of up to 5 runs, time measured inside the language by the shootout harness.
claimed_speedup: Mixed result. JRuby with invokedynamic is faster than CRuby 2.7.7 on 9 of 13 programs (derived from page data): binarytrees 1.24 s vs 6.75 s, fannkuchredux 1.19 s vs 4.34 s, nbody 14.85 s vs 43.56 s, spectralnorm 4.09 s vs 17.18 s, mandelbrot 7.12 s vs 16.74 s; slower on fasta (26.86 s vs 18.19 s), regexdna (9.49 s vs 6.25 s), revcomp (8.78 s vs 4.2 s) and about equal on matmul (18.9 s vs 18.39 s). Default JRuby (no invokedynamic) is faster on 8 of 13 and slower on matmul, nbody, fasta, regexdna, revcomp.
compiler_and_flags: jruby-dist 9.4.1.0 from Maven Central on the shootout's openjdk 19.0.1 image; run as `jruby -Xcompile.invokedynamic=true -S <file>` for the JRuby_InDy row (tools/languages.rb); CRuby 2.7.7 built with default configure plus --disable-install-doc.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, 80 GB DDR4-3200, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10
tradeoffs: Runs on the JVM (repo page: current branches need JRE 21 or newer), so JVM startup and memory apply: in the same shootout JRuby used about 1.2-2.1 GB on binarytrees versus 44.6 MB for CRuby. Repo page lists no global interpreter lock and tight Java integration.
caveats: Mixed evidence: JRuby loses to CRuby on several programs, so this is not a uniform speedup. Baseline is CRuby 2.7.7, not a current CRuby with YJIT (the shootout lists Ruby 3.2.1 rows separately). The shootout states its programs are chosen to be simplest, single-thread and without low-level hacks. Found by harvesting rows from a shootout; JRuby's own repo page only says it can be used 'as a faster version of Ruby' and gives no numbers.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'tracing JIT Python OR Ruby OR PHP faster than PyPy benchmark blog open source new JIT compiler 2026' surfaced kostya/jit-benchmarks; JRuby rows read from its README tables and tools/languages.rb.

name: OpenResty luajit2
workload: Compile speed of the edgelang-fan compiler (a program whose Lua is generated by the fanlang compiler) after using the fork's JIT-compilable table.clone API.
claimed_speedup: 'We observe 7% over-all speedup in the edgelang-fan compiler's compiling speed whose Lua is generated by the fanlang compiler' (README note under table.clone; no hardware, version or method given).
stars_or_usage: 1.4k stars; maintained branch used by OpenResty
tradeoffs: Fork carries OpenResty-specific Lua/C APIs (table.clone, table.isempty, table.nkeys, thread.exdata, lua_setexdata), larger JIT limits (maxtrace=8000, maxrecord=16000, maxmcode=40960 KB) and a SSE4.2 CRC32 string hash that only applies when built with -msse4.2. Branch is v2.1-agentzh.
caveats: Only quantitative claim is a single anecdote, and it is credited to the new table.clone API (the application had to be changed to call it), not to a general LuaJIT speedup; baseline version, workload size and machine are unstated. The CRC32 string-hash and larger JIT limits carry no numbers. Lua-side usage rather than C++, but the fork is a drop-in LuaJIT C library embeddable from C++.
found_via: Blogs / talks: followed the LuaJIT-fork thread from WebSearch 'Lua JIT faster than LuaJIT benchmark blog new implementation'; opened the github.com README and raw README.md.

name: mutable (WebAssembly/V8 query compiler)
workload: TPC-H queries (per the EDBT 2023 paper abstract quoted in the README): queries are JIT-compiled to WebAssembly and executed by the embedded V8 engine, which tiers unoptimized to optimized code while the query runs.
claimed_speedup: 'We are able to match or even outperform state-of-the-art systems like HyPer' (README quote of the EDBT 2023 abstract; no numbers on the page).
stars_or_usage: 118 stars; academic system from Saarland University
tradeoffs: Research main-memory DBMS ('for research and fast prototyping'); AGPL-3.0 licence; relies on an embedded V8 build for code generation and execution; query compilation is one feature among many.
caveats: Snippet only: the numbers live in the EDBT 2023 paper (the README's PDF link at bigdata.uni-saarland.de is EGRESS_BLOCKED here), so the tier is capped at C even though the paper is peer reviewed (a verifier who can read it should consider B). Claim is 'match or even outperform', not a uniform win. Baseline HyPer is a closed-source binary. The repo ships a benchmark harness (benchmark/README.md, nightly dashboard at cb.mutable.uni-saarland.de, blocked here) but no result table.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'JIT compiling query expressions faster than LLVM JIT database engineering blog benchmark TPC-H compile latency' (query-compilation topic), then github.com/mutable-org/mutable README.

name: Bun (JavaScriptCore) vs Node.js in plb2
language: Rust, TypeScript, JavaScript (repo page; plb2 measured Bun 1.0.20)
workload: plb2 programs implemented identically per language: nqueen (15-queens), matmul (two 1500x1500 matrices), sudoku (4000 hard puzzles, kudoku algorithm), bedcov (two arrays of 1,000,000 intervals, implicit interval trees); wall time in seconds via hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: Bun 1.0.20 vs Node 21.5.0, seconds (lower is better): nqueen 3.11 vs 3.73, matmul 1.75 vs 2.88, sudoku 3.07 vs 3.77, bedcov 2.32 vs 2.45; Bun faster on all four, matmul 1.65x (derived from page data). README text: Bun and Node 'are about twice as fast as PyPy'.
compiler_and_flags: Runtime versions stated (Bun 1.0.20, Node 21.5.0, Node-nojit row 21.5.0); no JIT flags stated, per-language build commands live in the repo's src directory (not opened).
hardware: Apple M1 MacBook Pro (hyperfine for timing)
tradeoffs: Bun is a JavaScriptCore-based runtime with its own bundler, test runner and package manager; semantics differ slightly from Node.
caveats: Evidence for an already-listed project. plb2 author is mostly a C programmer and says implementations in other languages may be suboptimal; startup and JIT warm-up (up to ~0.3 s) are included; one machine (Apple M1), old runtime versions (Bun 1.0.20, Node 21.5.0), last plb2 commit 2025-01-30. The gap is small on bedcov (2.32 vs 2.45). Bun's licence file also covers bundled third-party code (not checked).
found_via: Blogs / talks: plb2 (attractivechaos' programming-language benchmark, successor of his 2011 blog benchmark), found through the cross-language JIT shootout search.
